title: 15 Vegetables and Herbs That Yield the Highest When Grown in Pots Part 5
fullText: In our last video, we looked at 15 high yielding vegetables and herbs to grow in containers. Did you find that helpful? Today, I'm bringing you 15 more highly productive vegetables and herbs that can give you continuous harvests for months, all from just a single container. The very last vegetable on this list will especially surprise you with its mindblowing abundance. Now, let's grab a pot and get planting. At number 15, we have mashe, also known as corn salad. When traditional container greens begin to yellow and fade as the weather turns cold, most gardeners pack up their pots and think their growing season is over. But that is exactly when mache comes alive. This incredibly cold, hearty green thrives in freezing temperatures that would instantly kill other leafy plants, making it a highly productive crop for winter and early spring container gardening. Because it has a relatively shallow root system, a pot that is only 6 to 8 in deep is plenty of room. What makes mash so remarkably productive is its dense clustering growth habit. The rosettes stay compact, which means you can pack dozens of plants into a single wide container, maximizing every square in of potting soil. With just 4 hours of sunlight a day, you can start harvesting its soft spoon-shaped leaves in about 40 to 60 days. The secret to a high yield is using the cut and come again method. By delicately snipping the outer leaves and leaving the center of the rosette intact, a single container will keep producing fresh, nutty flavored salad greens straight through the coldest months of the year when your containers would otherwise be sitting empty and useless. Mosh proves that container productivity isn't just about how fast a plant grows in the summer, but how reliably it can feed you in the debt of winter. Did you know why machete is also called corn salad? In European history, before the invention of herbicides, this plant grew wild as a harmless weed in wheat and barley fields, collectively referred to as corn. Farmers of that era harvested them to make winter salads, transforming a simple weed into a highly sought-after vegetable in today's high-end restaurants. At number 14, we have pelane. Many people spend hours pulling pelane out of their garden beds, thinking it is nothing more than a stubborn, invasive weed. But cultivated pelane is actually an absolute powerhouse for container gardening. The secret to its massive productivity is its extreme tolerance for heat and drought. When midsummer temperatures soar and cause standard greens to wilt, bolt, and die, pelane actively explodes with growth. It requires a container about 8 in deep and absolutely loves full blistering sun. Its thick, succulent leaves and crunchy stems regenerate incredibly fast after being cut. Because it trails and naturally spills over the edges of a pot, a single container can produce a massive volume of edible greens, utilizing vertical space cascading down the sides of the planter. Aside from its aggressive growth rate, pelane is widely considered a superfood. It contains more omega-3 fatty acids than almost any other leafy vegetable on Earth. With a crisp, slightly citrusy crunch, it's absolutely perfect for summer salads, sandwiches, and smoothies. The most common mistake gardeners make is overwatering it. Pelane thrives on neglect. It earns its place on this list by proving that sometimes the most productive container crops are the resilient survivors that simply refuse to give up when the weather gets harsh. Pursane possesses a biological superpower called Cam photosynthesis. to retain water on hot dry days. It closes its stamata during the day and only opens them to absorb carbon dioxide at night. Interestingly, this process produces malic acid. If you harvest pelane early in the morning, the leaves will be significantly more tart and crisp compared to harvesting them in the late afternoon. At number 13, we have indive. If you want a leafy green that produces massive continuous volume in a strictly confined space, Indive is a top contender. At first glance, it might look like a standard fragile salad green, but endive is far more robust and heavily yielding. A container that is 8 to 10 in deep gives it plenty of room to develop a strong, deep root system. What truly earns Endive its place on this list is its impressive cut and come again capability paired with a long growing season. Instead of waiting weeks to harvest a single mature head and then having an empty pot, gardeners can continuously trim the outer frilly leaves. The plant quickly replaces whatever you take, creating a prolonged harvest season that can literally last for months. It performs exceptionally well in cooler weather and even tolerates partial shade, making it highly adaptable for balcony growers who don't get full afternoon sun. With its slightly bitter complex flavor that mellows beautifully when cooked or paired with a warm vinegrett, it adds incredible depth to fresh salads and hearty winter soups. A single container of Endive works like a steady factory, slowly but surely, outproducing crops that offer a one-time harvest. To reduce the characteristic bitterness of traditional French farmers use a technique called blanching. They tie the outer leaves together or place a pot over the plant to completely block sunlight from reaching the core. The lack of light prevents the plant from producing chlorophyll, resulting in a pale yellow, crisp, sweet core with a much more refined flavor. At number 12, we have sage. Most people are used to buying tiny, expensive plastic clamshells of sage at the grocery store for holiday cooking, never realizing how monstrously productive this herb can become when given a pot of its own. Sage is a woody perennial, meaning if you plant it once, it will reward you with harvest for years to come. Because it can grow into a substantial bush, a container that is at least 12 in deep is ideal to anchor its roots. Given full sun and well- draining soil, it produces thick, velvety leaves that can be harvested almost year round in milder climates. The true beauty of growing sage in a container is that frequent harvesting actually improves the plant. Trimming it regularly prevents the stems from becoming too woody, instead encouraging tender, highly flavorful new growth to flush out constantly. Its earthy, robust flavor is incredibly potent, meaning a single container will easily produce more than enough foliage for roasting meats, flavoring brown butter sauces, and stuffing poultry for years. While annuals require you to buy new seeds and soil every spring, a single pot of sage is a long-term investment that pays for itself a h 100 times over. The scientific name for sage is salvia, derived from the Latin word sal, which means to heal or to save. During the middle ages, this herb was highly revered as a cure all remedy. In fact, people in Europe used to share a famous proverb praising it. Why should a man die while sage grows in his garden? At number 11, we have amaranth greens. When the intense heat of August arrives, most leafy greens surrender, but amaranth is a tropical plant that transforms extreme heat into explosive leafy biomass. While some varieties of amaranth are grown primarily for their grain, the edible leaf varieties are a container gardener's secret weapon for unstoppable summer productivity. A 10 to 12in deep container placed in the hottest, sunniest spot on your patio will yield astonishing results. Within just 30 to 40 days of planting, you can start pinching off the vibrant green or striking red leaves. Here is where the magic happens. The more you harvest the top growth, the more the plant is forced to branch out laterally. This creates a massive bushy canopy of edible foliage from a single central stem. It cooks down beautifully, acting like a much sturdier, earthier version of traditional greens and is deeply valued in Asian, African, and Caribbean cuisines. Amaranth gives you a continuous heavy supply of highly nutritious greens exactly at the time of year when every other container plant in your garden is struggling to survive. Amaranth was once a sacred plant and a massive food source for the ancient Aztec civilization. They didn't just eat the leaves. They also popped amaranth seeds like popcorn, mixed them with honey, and sculpted them into statues of their gods. When the Spanish arrived in the Americas, they were so shocked and terrified by this custom that they banned the widespread cultivation of amaranth for centuries. So, we've just gone through our first five vegetables and herbs. Which one of these is your favorite? For me, the most impressive is Indive with its complex, slightly bitter flavor that beautifully mellows out when cooked and especially its ability to just keep on growing continuously. At number 10, we have thyme. At first glance, thyme doesn't look like a heavy yielder because its leaves are incredibly small. But what it lacks in individual leaf size, it more than makes up for in sheer volume, density, and culinary impact. Thyme is a spreading perennial that will quickly fill the entire surface of a container and beautifully cascade over the sides, creating a thick, fragrant mat. An 8-in deep pot with excellent drainage is perfect as time absolutely hates sitting in wet, soggy soil. Once established in full sun, it becomes a permanent food source. The secret to maximum yield is aggressive pruning. You can shear the entire plant back by a third and rather than dying, it will flush out with fresh, fragrant new growth within just a few weeks. Because the essential oils and flavors in thyme are so highly concentrated, a few small sprigs are all you need to dramatically elevate roasted vegetables, marinades, and slowcooked stews. Over the course of a single season, a modest pot of time produces an incredible amount of culinary power, making it one of the most spaceefficient plants you can possibly grow. Thanks to its high levels of thymol, a compound with incredibly potent natural antibacterial and antiseptic properties, thyme was used by ancient Egyptians as an essential ingredient in the mummification process. As for Roman soldiers, they regularly bathed in water infused with crushed thyme, fiercely believing that its scent would grant them extraordinary courage on the battlefield. At number nine, we have shuniku, also known as edible chrysanthemum. This incredibly fast growing Asian green is a highly productive crop that constantly surprises western gardeners who try it for the first time. A pot that is just 8 in deep is sufficient to support a dense planting of shungiku. It loves cooler weather and grows at an absolutely blistering pace. Often ready for its very first harvest in just 30 to 45 days. But the real secret to its high yield lies in how you harvest it. Instead of waiting for the plant to mature, experienced growers cut the main shoots when they are about 6 to 8 in tall, making sure to snip just above the lowest set of leaves. The plant responds to this cut by immediately sending out multiple side shoots, effectively multiplying your harvest with every single cut. With its unique, slightly floral and deeply herbaceious flavor, it is an absolute star ingredient in hot pots, quick stir fries, and warming soups. By utilizing this aggressive cut and come again method, a single container of shuniku can easily feed a family with fresh greens for weeks on end. In western countries, chrosanthemums are primarily bred as ornamental plants or used in ceremonies and funerals. But in East Asia, shungiku has been selectively bred for centuries purely for culinary purposes. Though they belong to the same plant family, shungiku is a prime example of how cultural differences can turn a vase flour into a premium ingredient for hot pots. At number eight, we have chives, also known as traditional onion chives. Not to be confused with garlic chives, traditional onion chives are one of the most reliable, high yielding perennial crops you can ever put in a pot. They are incredibly tough survivors, often being the very first green thing to wake up in the spring and the absolute last plant to die back in the freezing winter. A container 8 in deep will allow their bulbous roots to multiply year after year. The productivity of chives is staggering. Every single time you grab a handful and snip them down to the base, they rapidly shoot right back up. In a healthy container, you can easily get a halfozen heavy harvests from a single pot in one growing season. Their mild sweet onion flavor is perfect for baked potatoes, omelets, and garnishes. Even better, their beautiful purple flowers are completely edible, adding a sharp oniony bite to fresh salads. Because the clump naturally expands beneath the soil over time, your container will actually become more productive the longer you own it. Chibives are not only a delicious ingredient, but also a formidable bodyguard for your container garden. The sulfur compounds that give chives their distinct oniony scent can confuse and repel destructive pests like aphids or beetles. Many veteran gardeners always plant a pot of chives next to their roses or tomatoes to take advantage of this excellent biological defense barrier. At number seven, we have lemongrass. When people think of high yielding container crops, they rarely think of growing grass. But lemongrass is a phenomenal heavyduty producer in containers. You aren't just growing flimsy leaves. You growing dense, highly aromatic stocks that serve as the fundamental flavor base for countless Southeast Asian dishes. Because lemongrass forms a massive expanding clump, a larger container at least 12 to 14 in deep and equally as wide is strictly necessary. Give it full sun, intense heat, and plenty of water, and it will explode into a beautiful fountain-like display. The harvesting method is what makes it so productive. You harvest it by firmly snapping or cutting the thick outer stalks right at the soil line. By taking only the mature outer edges, the inner core of the clump simply keeps expanding and pushing out new stocks. One large healthy container of lemongrass will easily provide enough stocks for curries, soups, and fragrant teas for an entire year, producing physical weight and volume that puts many other herbs to shame. Everyone knows that lemongrass essential oil is great at repelling mosquitoes, but there is a surprising opposite truth. It is incredibly attractive to bees. The scent of lemongrass almost perfectly mimics the natural pherommones of honeybees. Because of this, beekeepers often rub lemongrass directly into new hives to gently lure an entire stray swarm into making it their new home. At number six, we have oregano. If you want a container crop that practically thrives on complete neglect while producing endless harvests, oregano is your plant. Much like thyme, it is an aggressive perennial that loves to spread and conquer space. An 8 to 10 in deep container gives it plenty of room to establish a dense fibrous root system. Interestingly, oregano actually prefers poor sandy soil and less water. Stressing the plant slightly by withholding water actually intensifies its pungent spicy flavor. The more aggressively you trim it, the bushier and more productive it becomes. What truly makes oregano a top tier producer on this list is that its flavor actually improves when dried. This means you can harvest the entire container multiple times throughout the summer, hang the stems upside down to dry, and stock your pantry with incredibly potent homegrown herbs. A single pot will easily provide enough oregano to flavor your homemade pizzas, pastas, and Mediterranean dishes straight through the winter months. The name oregano comes from two ancient Greek words, oros, mountain, and ganos, joy, translating to the incredibly romantic meaning joy of the mountain. The ancient Greeks believed that cows grazing on oregano covered hills would produce the tastiest meat. They also frequently planted this herb around graves to pray for eternal peace and happiness for the deceased. All right, we've made it through 10 vegetables and herbs on our list. Which one has impressed you the most? Drop your thoughts in the comments below. Next, we'll move on to the final five. Make sure to stick around until the very end because the last plant on this list is guaranteed to surprise you. At number five, we have gan, also known as Chinese broccoli. When most people think of growing broccoli, they automatically assume they need a massive garden bed and months of patience for a single head to form. But Guyan completely flips that script, turning a simple patio container into a continuous, high-yielding vegetable factory. Instead of waiting for a large crown to develop, this fast growing Asian green is cultivated for its thick, crunchy stems and tender leaves. A pot that is 8 to 10 in deep provides plenty of room for a dense cluster of plants. Gylon performs brilliantly in containers because its upright growth habit takes up very little horizontal space, allowing you to maximize the footprint of a small pot. With steady watering and decent sunlight, you can begin harvesting in just about 45 to 50 days. The true secret to its massive productivity is how it responds to being harvested. When you snap or cut the main thick stem for your evening stir fry, the plant immediately reacts by sending out multiple new lateral side shoots. This incredible cut and come again capability means a single container will continuously multiply your harvest, providing sweet, crisp vegetables week after week. Did you know that gylon is actually the parent of the expensive broccolini often found in western supermarkets? Broccolini is not just baby broccoli. It is a natural hybrid between traditional broccoli and gylon. This combination yields the thick floral fuettes of the west and the crunchy, sweet, completely stringless stems characteristic of Asia. At number four, we have turmeric. Turmeric asks the container gardener for nothing but patience, and in return, it delivers an enormous harvest hidden entirely beneath the soil. Above ground, turmeric is stunning, featuring broad, lush tropical leaves that look like high-end ornamental house plants. But in a wide container that is at least 12 in deep, an incredible multiplication process is happening out of sight. Plant a few small unassuming ryomes in the spring. Give them a warm, sunny spot and keep the soil consistently moist. After 8 to 10 months, when the weather cools and the foliage finally dies back, the real magic happens. You dump the pot upside down to reveal a massive interconnected cluster of bright orange, highly valuable turmeric roots. You can easily yield several pounds of roots from a single container. You harvest what you need to make anti-inflammatory teas, golden milk, and vibrant curries and simply save a few small pieces in a cool, dark place to replant in the spring, starting the highly productive cycle all over again. Turmeric is not just a superfood. It is also a fantastic natural chemical indicator right in your kitchen. Turmeric powder contains curcumin which is normally bright yellow, but if you mix it with an alkaline substance such as baking soda or soap, the yellow color will instantly turn to brick red. Historically, it was also the sacred dye used to create the traditional saffron robes of Buddhist monks. At number three, we have ginger. Much like its cousin turmeric, ginger is a subterranean powerhouse that actually performs exceptionally well in containers. In fact, many experienced gardeners argue that containers are better for ginger than traditional garden beds. Containers heat up faster in the sun and they allow you to use loose, highly well- draining potting soil, which ginger ryomes desperately need to expand easily without fighting compacted clay. A wide shallow container about 10 to 12 in deep is ideal because ginger naturally grows horizontally rather than downward. With partial shade and consistent moisture, a single cheap piece of store-bought ginger can multiply its own weight five or 10 times over a single growing season. But the absolute best part of container grown ginger is that you don't even have to harvest it all at once. You can simply dig around the edge of the pot, snap off a fresh spicy piece for your evening stir fry, cover it back up with dirt, and leave the rest of the plant growing happily. Queen Elizabeth I 1 of England is actually credited with inventing the famous gingerbread man. To impress foreign dignitaries and high-ranking guests visiting her court, she ordered the royal bakers to use expensive ginger dough to shape cookies that mirrored the exact likeness of those very guests as a highly creative diplomatic gift. At number two, we have Jerusalem Martichokes, also known as sun chokes. If you want to talk about raw, heavy physical tonnage from a single container, sun chokes are nearly unbeatable. These are towering sunflower-like plants that can easily reach 6 to 8 ft tall. But the true prize is not the flowers. It is the massive root system below. Because of their sheer size, you need a large container at least 15 to 18 in deep and wide. Plant a few small tubers in the spring, and by late autumn, the plant will have generated dozens of crisp, nutty flavored tubers, tightly packed beneath the soil. The yield from a single large pot is staggering, often providing enough food to act as a staple carbohydrate for weeks. You can roast them, mash them like potatoes, or slice them raw into salads for an incredible crunch. But be warned, sun chokes are incredibly vigorous. If you leave even a tiny piece of a tuber in that soil, it will aggressively regrow the following year. They are a true survival crop, offering unmatched caloric yield for a container environment. The name Jerusalem artichokes is a spectacular linguistic deception. They have absolutely nothing to do with the city of Jerusalem and they are definitely not artichokes. In reality, they are a species of sunflower native to North America. The word Jerusalem is believed to be a misprononunciation by the English of the Italian word jer sole meaning sunflower. Furthermore, their tubers store energy as inulin instead of regular starch. At number one, we have lemon balm. This is a plant that completely changes the conversation about container productivity. Lemon balm is a close relative in the mint family, and it possesses the exact same unstoppable, almost frightening vigor. In fact, you should never plant lemon balm directly in the ground because it spreads rapidly through underground runners and will ruthlessly conquer your entire yard. But when you take all of that aggressive survivalist energy and confine it strictly to a 12-in container, the result is the most wildly productive herb you can possibly grow. With decent sunlight and regular watering, it grows at an explosive rate. You can literally take a pair of scissors, cut the entire plant down to the dirt, and it will aggressively flush back into a massive bushy dome of leaves in just a matter of weeks. The cycle never stops. It produces an endless, heavy supply of bright lemons foliage that is absolutely perfect for calming herbal teas, infused syrups, cocktails, and fruit salads. What truly makes lemon balm the undeniable number one is its sheer volume, unmatched resilience, and the fact that it is a plant so highly productive, putting it in a container is the only way to tame it. Historically, lemon balm was known as the herb of gladness. In the 14th century, French nuns used it as the main ingredient to create carmealite water, a wildly famous herbal tincture. European nobility and royalty consumed it daily because they absolutely believed that this tonic could cure headaches, dispel melancholy, and promote a long, joyful life. So, we've just gone through the first 15 fantastic picks for your container garden. Which vegetable or herb impressed you the most? Let me know down in the comments. But don't go anywhere just yet because this list is far from over. Right now, let's dive into the next 15 vegetables and herbs. the true yield champions that promise to transform your small space into a lush garden you can harvest all year round. Let's get started. At number 15, we have cilantro. Most people don't think of cilantro as a high yield container crop because they usually buy it in small bunches from the grocery store and assume it doesn't produce very much. But experienced container gardeners know that cilantro can become one of the most productive herbs in a small space when grown correctly. The secret is not growing one large plant, but growing many plants together in a single container. A pot that is at least 8 to 10 in deep and 10 to 12 in wide can support dozens of cilantro plants, creating a dense patch of edible foliage. One of the biggest reasons cilantro earns a place on this list is speed. While many vegetables require months before the first harvest, cilantro can often be harvested in as little as 30 to 45 days after planting. That quick turnaround makes it especially rewarding for beginners who want fast results. It grows best with 4 to 6 hours of sunlight per day and performs particularly well during the cooler temperatures of spring and fall. In hot summer conditions, cilantro tends to bolt quickly, which is one of the most common mistakes gardeners make. Fortunately, containers provide a major advantage because they can be moved into partial shade during the hottest part of the day, extending the harvest period. Another reason cilantro is so productive is succession planting. Many experienced growers sew a new batch of seeds every 2 or 3 weeks. By the time one container is reaching peak production, another is already developing behind it. And unlike some crops that only get used occasionally, cilantro is something many people use every week. It adds flavor to tacos, curries, soups, noodle dishes, rice bowls, salsas, salads, and countless other recipes. Because it is harvested frequently and grows back quickly, the total amount produced from a few containers can be surprisingly large. What makes cilantro deserve its place on this list is not the size of any single harvest, but the combination of rapid growth, dense planting, frequent use, and repeated production. A simple container of cilantro can provide fresh herbs for meal after meal, proving that even one small pot can become a remarkably productive food growing system. At number 14, we have dill. Most gardeners grow dill for its fresh flavor, but few realize how much productivity can come from a single container. At first glance, dill doesn't look like a high yield crop. Its thin stems and delicate feathery leaves appear almost fragile compared to many vegetable. But what makes dill special is that nearly every stage of its growth produces something useful. A container that is at least 10 to 12 in deep provides enough room for healthy root development, while 6 or more hours of direct sunlight each day encourages vigorous growth. Within about 40 to 60 days after planting, gardeners can begin harvesting the fragrant leaves. But that's only the beginning. As the season progresses, dill produces flowerheads that are highly valued for pickling. and later those flowers develop into seeds that can be harvested and stored as a spice. Few container crops offer three separate harvest opportunities from a single planting. Another reason dill ranks so highly is its ability to recede itself. If some mature seeds are allowed to fall back into the container, new dill plants often emerge on their own. What begins as a single crop can gradually turn into multiple generations growing in the same pot. This self-renewing habit dramatically increases long-term productivity with very little effort from the gardener. Dill also grows vertically rather than spreading outward, making it an efficient use of limited space. Even a small balcony or patio can support several containers without feeling crowded. Beyond the harvest itself, dill contributes to the overall health of a container garden by attracting pollinators and beneficial insects when it flowers. These insects help support nearby crops and improve the productivity of the entire growing area. One of the most common mistakes people make is choosing containers that are too shallow, which can limit root development and reduce plant vigor. With proper depth, sunlight, and regular watering, dill often grows taller and more productive than most people expect. What makes dill deserve its place on this list is its incredible efficiency. It produces edible leaves, flowers, and seeds, frequently replants itself, attracts beneficial insects, and requires very little space to do it. A single container can continue providing value long after many other herbs have finished their season, making dill one of the hardest working plants a container gardener can grow. At number 13, we have parsley. This is one of the most underestimated herbs in container gardening because most people think of it as nothing more than a garnish. They see a few sprigs on a plate and assume it has little value beyond decoration. But gardeners who grow parsley quickly discover that it can become one of the most productive plants in their entire container garden. A pot that is 8 to 10 in deep provides enough room for strong root development. And with 4 to 6 hours of sunlight each day, parsley can produce a steady supply of leaves for months. Unlike many vegetables that are harvested once and removed, parsley thrives on a cut and regrow cycle. The key is to harvest only the outer stems while leaving the center of the plant untouched. This encourages continuous new growth and allows the same plant to remain productive throughout the season. Most varieties are ready for their first harvest in about 60 to 70 days. But once production begins, the harvest can continue for a remarkably long time. One of the reasons parsley is so valuable is that it fits into almost every kitchen. Because it is used so frequently, gardeners often find themselves harvesting from the same container several times each week. That regular use transforms parsley from a simple herb into a dependable food crop. Another advantage is its adaptability. Parsley tolerates cooler temperatures better than many herbs and can continue growing when more heat sensitive crops begin to struggle. Container growing also allows gardeners to maintain consistent soil moisture, which parsley loves. One of the most common mistakes is cutting the entire plant at once. While this may provide a larger immediate harvest, it significantly reduces long-term productivity. Experienced growers know that smaller, more frequent harvests produce far more food over the course of a season. A healthy parsley plant can provide dozens of harvests before it finally slows down. At number 12, we have mustard greens. If you're looking for a crop that makes a container look productive in the shortest amount of time possible, mustard greens are hard to beat. Many gardeners are shocked by how quickly these plants grow. A container that seemed nearly empty a few weeks earlier can suddenly be overflowing with large edible leaves ready for harvest. That's one of the biggest reasons mustard greens earn a place on this list. They combine fast growth, repeated harvests, and impressive yields from a relatively small space. Most varieties grow well in containers that are at least 8 to 10 in deep and receive 4 to 6 hours of sunlight each day. Under favorable conditions, gardeners can begin harvesting leaves in as little as 30 to 40 days after planting. Another advantage is the size of the harvest. Unlike many herbs that produce small leaves, mustard greens develop broad foliage that can fill bowls, stir fries, soups, and salads with just a few cutings. This makes each harvest feel substantial. One of the secrets to maximizing production is using the cut and come again method. Instead of pulling the entire plant, gardeners harvest only the larger outer leaves while allowing the center to continue growing. The plant responds by producing new foliage, creating a cycle of continuous harvests that can last for weeks or even months. Frequent harvesting actually encourages additional growth, making the container more productive over time. Mustard greens also perform exceptionally well during cool weather, making them ideal for spring and fall gardening when many summer crops are not yet producing. Their slightly peppery flavor becomes milder when harvested young and stronger as the leaves mature, giving gardeners flexibility in how they use the crop. One common mistake is overcrowding plants in a container. While mustard greens can be planted fairly densely, excessive crowding reduces air flow and limits leaf size. Giving each plant enough room allows it to reach its full productive potential. Another advantage of mustard greens is their nutritional value. The leaves are rich in vitamins's A, C, and K, making them one of the healthiest crops. s a container gardener can grow. At number 11, we have Tatsoy. At first glance, Tatsoy may not look like one of the highest yielding crops you can grow in a container. Its low growing rosette of dark green leaves appears compact and modest compared to larger vegetables. But that's exactly what makes it such an efficient producer. Tatsoy excels at turning a small amount of space into a surprisingly large amount of food. Because the plants remain compact, they can be grown much closer together than many other greens, allowing gardeners to fit more plants into a single container. A pot that is only 6 to 8 in deep is usually sufficient, making tatsoy an excellent choice for balconies, patios, and other limited growing area. One of the reasons Tatsoy ranks so highly is its speed. Under good growing conditions, it can be ready for harvest in as little as 25 to 40 days. That means gardeners don't have to wait long before seeing results. With 4 to 6 hours of sunlight each day and consistently moist soil, Tatsoy develops dense clusters of spoon-shaped leaves that are both attractive and highly productive. Another advantage is its cut and come again growth habit. Instead of harvesting the entire plant, gardeners can remove the larger outer leaves while leaving the center intact. This allows the plant to continue producing fresh foliage for multiple harvest cycles. Over time, the total amount harvested from a single container can be surprisingly impressive. Tatsoy also thrives during cooler weather, making it one of the best crops for extending the productivity of a container garden into spring and fall. While many vegetables slow down or struggle when temperatures drop, tatsoy often continues producing highquality leaves, this resilience makes it particularly valuable for gardeners looking to maximize food production throughout the year. One common mistake gardeners make is overwatering. Although tats soy appreciates consistent moisture, waterlogged soil can lead to root problems and reduced growth. Using a well- draining potting mix helps maintain healthy plants and steady production. At number 10, we have mazuna. This is one of those crops that often surprises gardeners because it doesn't look particularly impressive when it's first planted. The seedlings are small, delicate, and easy to overlook. But once mizuna gets established, it can become one of the most productive leafy greens in a container garden. What makes it so valuable is its remarkable ability to regrow after harvest. While some vegetables produce a single crop and then decline, Mizuna seems determined to keep generating new leaves every time it's cut. That's exactly why experienced gardeners love it. A container only 6 to 8 in deep is usually enough to support healthy plants, making Mizuna an excellent choice for small balconies, patios, and urban gardens where space is limited. One of its biggest advantages is speed. Under favorable conditions, gardeners can begin harvesting leaves in as little as 20 to 30 days after planting. Few leafy vegetables deliver usable food so quickly. With four to 6 hours of sunlight each day and consistent watering, Mizuna develops dense clusters of deeply cut leaves that create an abundant appearance in a surprisingly short period of time. The real productivity comes from its cut and come again nature. Instead of harvesting the entire plant, gardeners remove the outer leaves and leave the center growing. New foliage quickly replaces what was harvested, allowing the same container to provide multiple harvests over an extended period. Frequent harvesting actually helps encourage more growth, turning a single planting into a long-term source of fresh greens. One common mistake is waiting too long to harvest. Older leaves can become tougher, while regular cutting encourages tender new growth and higher overall production. At number nine, we have sorrel. This is one of the most underrated edible plants in container gardening, largely because many people have never heard of it. Yet, among experienced gardeners, sorrel is often considered one of the most productive long-term crops you can grow in a pot. Unlike many leafy greens that need to be replanted every season, sorrel is a perennial in many climates, which means a single planting continue producing for years.
